passage:
Saturday. When Uday came to collect his last boxes, Pallavi went to her room and shut the door. She heard him ask her mother, "Is she still not talking to me?" She turned her music louder. It was his fault. She had decided that.

The following Friday. Her grandmother found her staring at a photo of the three of them at the beach. "You're angry." "Yes." "Anger is often sadness wearing armour, and grown-up marriages are more tangled than they look from outside." Pallavi said nothing, but she didn't put the photo away.

The Sunday after. Uday knocked. She opened the door. "I'm not ready to talk about it," she said. "But you can ask me about my exam." He sat on the bed's far end and asked. She answered, and it was the first time in weeks she hadn't left the room.

qa.q: What was Pallavi looking at when her grandmother found her?
qa.a: She was staring at a photo of the three of them at the beach.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel toward her father on the first Saturday, and what might lie under it?
qa.a: She felt angry and blamed him, and her grandmother suggested the anger could be covering sadness.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do on the last Sunday that kept the door open without forcing things?
qa.a: She said she wasn't ready to talk about the divorce but let him ask about her exam, staying in the room with him.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when he stood outside his daughter's shut door?
qa.a: Probably hurt and worried about losing her, since he asked her mother about her and later came back and knocked again.

grounding: Shows a teen blaming a parent and leaving the room, then recognising the sadness under the anger and letting the parent back in slowly.

passage:
Jomon, sit. You slammed the door on your father this morning, and I know that feeling well.
When I was sixteen, my parents separated. I decided it was all my father's fault. He had been the one who shouted, so to me he was the villain. On his visits I went up to the terrace and stayed there until his scooter left. For a whole year I would not sit in one room with him.
Then my Chithi, my mother's younger sister, found me up there one evening. She asked, "Rashmi, are you angry, or are you sad?" I started to say angry, and burst into tears instead.
Later I learned there were things neither of them had told me, on both sides. I still don't know the whole story, and that's fine. What I know is this: I nearly lost a father over a story I had half-written myself.

qa.q: Where did young Rashmi go during her father's visits?
qa.a: Up to the terrace, until his scooter left.

qa.q: What was young Rashmi really feeling beneath the anger?
qa.a: She was deeply sad about the separation; when Chithi asked her, she burst into tears, showing the anger was covering grief.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed things for Rashmi, and why?
qa.a: Chithi's question, angry or sad, made Rashmi see her sadness and begin to accept that her parents' story was more complicated than she knew.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's father have felt during that year?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and shut out, arriving on his scooter again and again only to find his daughter gone to the terrace.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming one parent during a divorce, realising anger covered sadness and adult relationships were complex, and not cutting him off.

passage:
The bus strike meant there was only one way to reach cousin Tanu's engagement in Nagpur: three hours in Papa's small car. Madhuri took the back seat, as far from him as possible, earphones in and music off.
Since he moved out, she had refused every dinner with him. He broke our home, she kept telling herself.
Halfway there, a lorry jammed the highway and they stopped dead. In the silence, her brother Chetan, twelve, started crying. "Why can't we just talk normally?"
Papa's hands tightened on the wheel. He looked old, Madhuri thought suddenly, and tired, not like a villain.
She took out one earphone. The anger felt thinner than it had at home, and underneath it was something heavier, a sadness she hadn't let herself feel.
"I'm not ready to talk about it," she said. "But I'll come for dinner on Sunday." Papa nodded without turning around.

qa.q: Why did the family have to travel in Papa's car?
qa.a: Because of the bus strike, the car was the only way to reach cousin Tanu's engagement in Nagpur.

qa.q: What feeling did Madhuri discover underneath her anger?
qa.a: She noticed a heavier sadness she had not let herself feel, and saw her father as old and tired instead of a villain.

qa.q: Which choice did Madhuri make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She agreed to Sunday dinner while saying she was not ready to talk, keeping the door open instead of cutting Papa off completely.

qa.q: How does Chetan experience the silent car ride?
qa.a: Chetan feels upset and stuck between them; the silence becomes too much and he cries, asking why they cannot just talk normally.

grounding: A teen who blames her father for the divorce senses the sadness under her anger and chooses not to cut him off.
